extracted.intended_audience: mathematics and computer-science students, researchers, and authors preparing proofs, papers, theses, literate programs, or technical documentation
extracted.subtask_short: mathematical writing for math and CS
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing mathematics and computer-science documents (proofs, papers, theses, programs, manuals), emphasizing exposition, notation, typography, and organization. Derived from Stanford CS209 lecture notes on mathematical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate symbols in different formulas by words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols in different formulas must be separated by words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Consider Sq, q p.'  Good: 'Consider Sq, where q < p.' — Always put words between adjacent formula fragments so the reader can parse relations between formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't start a sentence with a symbol (e.g., a mathematical symbol or formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'xn - a has n distinct zeroes.'  Good: 'The polynomial xn - a has n distinct zeroes.' — Begin sentences with words to aid flow and parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical shorthand symbols in running prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use shorthand logical symbols like ∴, ∃, ∀, V, 3, 3; — replace them by the corresponding words (except in works on logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words instead of shorthand symbols in normal mathematical exposition so sentences remain readable to general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-in sentence before theorem/algorithm must be complete or end with colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement just preceding a theorem, algorithm, etc., should be a complete sentence or should end with a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'We now have the following' followed immediately by 'Theorem. H(x) is continuous.' — Instead write a complete lead-in like 'We can now prove the following result.' and make theorem statements self-contained and informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem/statement should be self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of a theorem should usually be self-contained, not depending on assumptions in the preceding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restate necessary hypotheses inside the theorem statement so the reader need not scan previous paragraphs to understand the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' judiciously to avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the word 'we' often to avoid passive voice, but only when it genuinely means 'you and me together'; avoid using 'I' in most technical writing unless the author's persona is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'We' creates a dialog with the reader; if multiple authors or an individual author requires disambiguation, add clarifying text (e.g., 'one of the authors (DEK)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sentence rhythm and flow; read aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a definite rhythm in sentences; read what you have written and change wording if it does not flow smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose among synonyms (e.g., 'merge patterns' vs 'merging patterns') to preserve cadence; don't omit words that help parsing (e.g., 'that') when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow 'assume'/'suppose' with 'that' when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'assume' and 'suppose' should usually be followed by 'that' unless another 'that' appears nearby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'We have that x = ...' — instead say 'We have x = ...'. Avoid unnecessary padding like 'because of the fact that'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure, use parallelism
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary sentence structure and choice of words to avoid monotony; use parallelism when parallel concepts are being discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetitive sentence starters ('Thus, ... Consequently, ... Therefore, ...') unless rhythm or emphasis calls for it; parallel form helps clarity when enumerating related items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid homework-style formula lists; provide running commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use the style of homework papers where a sequence of formulas is merely listed; tie concepts together with running commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why steps are done, give transitional sentences, and guide the reader through chains of formulas instead of expecting them to infer connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: State definitions/important items twice (complementary ways); define variables at first use
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to state things twice, in complementary ways (especially definitions). All variables must be defined, at least informally, when first introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary restatement (formal and informal, or symbolic and verbal) reinforces understanding; give intuitive description alongside formal definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate the reader and keep reader-model in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivate the reader for what follows and keep the reader uppermost in mind: what they know so far and what they expect next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain reasons why a lemma/definition is considered and avoid overclaiming ('interesting') without showing why; be humble when describing your own work (avoid superlatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write so sentences still make sense if formulas are skimmed
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers will skim over formulas on first reading; sentences should flow smoothly when formulas are replaced by placeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure surrounding prose explains ideas independent of heavy symbolic detail so skimmers can follow the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent notation; don't reuse symbols for different things
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use the same notation for two different things; conversely, use consistent notation for the same thing when it appears in several places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose index naming conventions (e.g., i from 1..n, j from 1..m) and typographic conventions (lowercase for elements, uppercase for sets) to reduce reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts and avoid over-indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get carried away by subscripts; avoid subscripted subscripts when unnecessary; don't name set elements unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use set element notation rather than heavy indexing if it simplifies exposition; reduce visual clutter to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important formulas on a separate line and number selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Display important formulas on a line by themselves. Number the most important displayed formulas only (not every formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give reference numbers to formulas you will refer to later; avoid numbering trivial displayed expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sentences unambiguous left-to-right
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should be readable from left to right without ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'Smith remarked in a paper about the scarcity of data' which can be parsed in multiple ways; rephrase to disambiguate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell small numbers as words when adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Small numbers should be spelled out when used as adjectives, but not when used as names (i.e., when talking about numbers as numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: 'Method 2 is illustrated in Fig. 1; it requires 17 passes.' Bad: 'The method requires 2 passes.' — be consistent and clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize theorem/lemma/algorithm names in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names like Theorem 1, Lemma 2, Algorithm 3, Method 4 in headings and titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization consistently to signal numbered results and improve navigability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind common style pitfalls (prepositions, participles, fragments, agreement, commas, split infinitives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch out for prepositions at sentence end, dangling participles, sentence fragments, pronoun agreement, unnecessary commas, and split infinitives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are common problems to inspect and fix during revision; but also apply judgment rather than slavish rule-following (some split infinitives or sentence-ending prepositions are acceptable for clarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary colons before displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overdo the use of colons; omit colons when the following displayed formula completes the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a colon if the text introduces a list or a full sentence follows; otherwise let the sentence flow into the displayed formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening paragraph and first sentence should be best
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening paragraph should be your best paragraph, and its first sentence should be your best sentence; a bad start discourages readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weak openings like 'An x is y.' — instead hook the reader with motivation, context, and a clear statement of importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation rules with quotations and parentheses should be logical
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow conventional English rules for commas and periods inside quotation marks, but keep punctuation strictly logical with respect to parentheses and brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put a period inside parentheses if and only if the parenthesized sentence is a complete sentence; punctuation within parentheses should be correct if the parenthesized statement is removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long noun-strings and unnecessary jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist long strings of nouns used as adjectives; avoid jargon unnecessarily — prefer a nonspecialist's vocabulary where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., reword 'packet switched data communication network protocol problem' to clearer phrasing; when in doubt, simplify language for wider readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and good sources of style (read sample good writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When in doubt, read examples of excellent technical writing (e.g., The Art of Computer Programming) and use examples to model good exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief, relevant quotations sparingly; humor should be used only when it depends on the reader's technical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with typographic tools and fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overuse typographic devices (many fonts, excessive bold/italics); typographic tools can be overdone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic conventions judiciously and consistently; avoid distracting style choices that disrupt reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and ellipsis conventions in formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with spacing around ellipses and dots in formulas; place commas before and after ellipses where appropriate and choose vertical alignment of dots depending on surrounding symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The character string '. . . ;' looks strange because of spacing; typesetting systems may help, but authors must check spacing manually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid linebreaks in the middle of formulas; tie symbols to words
rubrics_metrics.description: Linebreaks in the middle of formulas are undesirable; avoid 'psychologically bad' line breaks that leave final symbols isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TeX features (e.g., ties ~, penalties) or other formatting tools to keep related tokens together and prevent awkward breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct TeX/typographic commands for symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: When using TeX, use the appropriate commands for symbols (e.g., \mid, \emptyset) instead of ad-hoc character choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct commands produce proper spacing and semantics; learn your typesetting system to avoid subtle spacing/semantic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader what you're doing with brief signposts
rubrics_metrics.description: Include brief comments like 'We demonstrate the second conclusion by contradiction,' or 'There must be a witness...' to tell the reader what is going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signposting helps reader synchronization with goals, subgoals, and proof strategies; mix exposition-level comments with technical steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent and intentional with tense usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Either use present tense throughout or write sequentially; avoid mixing tenses awkwardly on the same subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present-tense gives a timeless exposition; sequential tense is useful for long papers with narrative structure — choose a scheme and apply it consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid proof by contradiction when a direct proof exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer direct proofs when available; proof by contradiction is often the easiest for the solver but may not give the best exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct argumentation when it clarifies structure and avoids unnecessary detours that confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make paragraph breaks and starts clear when using displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure it is clear where new paragraphs begin, especially when using displayed formulas which can blur paragraph boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spacing, introductory phrases, or textual markers to indicate paragraph transitions so readers do not lose the thread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose notation appropriate to the audience (programming vs mathematical notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between programming-language notation and mathematical notation; use the notation appropriate to formal papers rather than program text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., avoid array-index notation p[r] in papers; prefer p_r or subscripts; avoid '*' for multiplication in printed math — use juxtaposition or centered dot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize nested parentheses and awkward punctuation clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive nested parentheses and coincident punctuation; where two punctuation marks coincide, follow conventional rules (write one comma, keep period, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nested parentheses are unavoidable, consider using brackets or reformulating the sentence; typographers may adjust outer-parenthesis sizing to help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use typographic and notational conventions to aid readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use boldface, arrows, roman type for superscripts like 'st' appropriately and only when appropriate to audience; choose conventions that clarify semantics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, use roman type for ordinal indicators to avoid confusion with powers; choose vector notation consistent with field conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in comparative and technical vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise wording when technical distinctions matter (e.g., 'not nonincreasing' vs 'increasing' — they are different).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sloppy synonyms that change meaning; clarify quantifiers and order relations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotony of sentence openings but preserve parallelism when intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get hung up on one or two styles of sentence openings (e.g., 'Thus, ... Consequently, ...') but use parallelism when the sentence's point requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary phrasing to maintain reader interest while using parallel structure to emphasize related items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization: prioritize structure and avoid distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do organize material thoughtfully; avoid distractions (irrelevant notation, odd prose) that detract from communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization is more than linear order; weave branches and threads together coherently. 'Anything that helps communication is good; anything that hurts is bad.' — Paul Halmos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of audience conventions about hyphenation and compound nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound noun hyphenation (e.g., 'programming-language notation') depends on audience norms; in CS some compounds are commonly unhyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt conventions common in your field to avoid awkward hyphenation that reads wrong to insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use copy editors and professional designers when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not forget the value of professionals (copy editors, book designers) in preparing polished books and long documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional help improves typography, margins, fonts, and overall readability; plan for editorial revision beyond author self-publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with exclamation points and other emphatics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use exclamation points only where appropriate; many style authorities recommend avoiding them except for real exclamations or interjections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of exclamation points distracts; tricks like parenthesized '(!)' can be used sparingly for effect but rely on judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose pronoun conventions with consistency and awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose how to handle gendered pronouns (he, they, he or she) consistently and be aware of audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different readers and authorities prefer different solutions; be explicit about your choice and follow it throughout the document.
